purpose: Bounded Marrow ED8 Anatomy Chapter 9 explanation rollout. Raw imported source remains immutable; this file contains learner-facing augmentation only.

marrow__ANAT_CH09_Q001.takeaway: The spinal cord develops from the narrow caudal part of the neural tube.
marrow__ANAT_CH09_Q001.displayText:
The spinal cord develops from the caudal part of the neural tube.

The nervous system develops from the neuroectoderm i.e. the specialized ectoderm overlying the notochord. The neuroectoderm initially thickens to form the neural plate. The neural plate is then converted to a neural groove, followed by a neural tube.

• The enlarged cranial part of neural tube forms the brain. It has 3 primary vesicles that form:
  • Forebrain (prosencephalon)
  • Midbrain (mesencephalon)
  • Hindbrain (rhombencephalon)
• The narrow caudal part of the neural tube forms the spinal cord.

rationales.b: The notochord induces overlying ectoderm to become neuroectoderm but does not itself form the spinal cord.
rationales.c: The primitive streak is involved in gastrulation and germ-layer formation, not direct formation of the spinal cord.
rationales.d: The rhombencephalon is the hindbrain portion of the cranial neural tube and gives rise to pons, cerebellum and medulla rather than spinal cord.

marrow__ANAT_CH09_Q002.takeaway: Anterior and posterior neuropores temporarily connect the neural-tube lumen with the amniotic cavity.
marrow__ANAT_CH09_Q002.displayText:
The neuropores facilitate communication between the neural tube and the amniotic cavity.

The neural plate first becomes tubular in the middle. The cranial and caudal ends of the neural tube remain open and are called the anterior and posterior neuropores, respectively.

The neuropores facilitate communication between the neural tube and the amniotic cavity. Amniotic fluid provides nutrition to the developing neuroectodermal cells before the circulatory system is established.

rationales.b: The yolk sac communicates with the embryonic gut through the vitelline duct, not with the neural tube through neuropores.
rationales.c: The allantois is an endodermal diverticulum associated with the connecting stalk and is not continuous with the neural-tube lumen.
rationales.d: The uterine cavity is not the direct embryologic space into which the neuropores open; they open into the amniotic cavity.

marrow__ANAT_CH09_Q003.takeaway: The anterior neuropore closes near day 25 and its adult landmark is the lamina terminalis.
marrow__ANAT_CH09_Q003.displayText:
The location of the anterior neuropore is represented in adults as lamina terminalis.

The anterior neuropore closes around the 25th day of intrauterine life. Its location in adults is represented by the lamina terminalis. The lamina terminalis forms the anterior boundary of the third ventricle.

The posterior neuropore closes around the 28th day of intrauterine life. Its location in adults is represented by the terminal ventricle. The terminal ventricle is an expansion of the central canal in the lower conus medullaris, just above the filum terminale.
emphasis: anterior boundary of the third ventricle

rationales.a: The septum transversum contributes importantly to the diaphragm and is unrelated to the adult landmark of the anterior neuropore.
rationales.b: The terminal ventricle represents the site of the posterior neuropore, not the anterior neuropore.
rationales.d: The foramen of Monro connects each lateral ventricle with the third ventricle and is not the adult remnant of a neuropore.

marrow__ANAT_CH09_Q004.takeaway: The medulla derives from the myelencephalon, the caudal subdivision of the rhombencephalon.
marrow__ANAT_CH09_Q004.displayText:
In infantile progressive bulbar palsy, the affected structure is the medulla oblongata. It arises from the rhombencephalon (hindbrain).

The rhombencephalon is further subdivided into a cranial part (metencephalon) and a caudal part (myelencephalon).
• Metencephalon - forms the pons and cerebellum
• Myelencephalon - forms the medulla oblongata

rationales.a: The prosencephalon forms forebrain derivatives such as the telencephalon and diencephalon, not the medulla.
rationales.b: The mesencephalon persists as the midbrain and does not form the medulla oblongata.
rationales.d: A defined embryologic precursor exists: the medulla arises from myelencephalon within the rhombencephalon.

marrow__ANAT_CH09_Q005.takeaway: The flexure between metencephalon and myelencephalon is the pontine flexure.
marrow__ANAT_CH09_Q005.displayText:
The flexure between the metencephalon and the myelencephalon is called the pontine flexure.

The prosencephalon, mesencephalon, and rhombencephalon are initially arranged craniocaudally. Due to differential growth of different regions of the brain, various flexures form between them.

Note: A deep furrow called the rhombencephalic isthmus separates the mesencephalon from the metencephalon.

rationales.a: The cephalic flexure occurs in the midbrain region rather than between metencephalon and myelencephalon.
rationales.b: Mesencephalic flexure is another name used for the cephalic flexure and therefore is not the hindbrain flexure asked here.
rationales.d: Cerebellar flexure is not the named embryologic flexure separating the metencephalon from myelencephalon.

marrow__ANAT_CH09_Q006.takeaway: Sulcus limitans separates the sensory alar plate dorsally from the motor basal plate ventrally.
marrow__ANAT_CH09_Q006.displayText:
The sulcus limitans is located between the sensory alar and the motor basal plates.

The cells in the wall of the neural tube proliferate and are subdivided into the inner mantle layer and outer marginal layer. Due to the fast growth of the mantle layer cells, the lumen of the neural tube gets compressed.

The line separating the compressed ventral part from the dorsal part is called the sulcus limitans. When the sulcus limitans is formed, the tube is divided into the dorsal or alar lamina and ventral or basal lamina.

In the spinal cord, the ventral thickenings or basal plates contain ventral motor horn cells. The dorsal thickenings i.e. the alar plates contain the interneurons that receive the terminals of primary sensory neurons.

rationales.a: The interpeduncular fossa is a surface feature of the midbrain and does not define the embryologic alar-basal boundary.
rationales.c: The pontomedullary junction separates pons from medulla; the sulcus limitans instead separates alar and basal plates longitudinally.
rationales.d: The hypothalamic sulcus separates thalamus from hypothalamus; it is not the sulcus limitans.

marrow__ANAT_CH09_Q007.takeaway: The keyed exception is the hypoglossal motor nucleus, a basal-plate derivative; the source classifies the other listed nuclei as alar-plate derivatives.
marrow__ANAT_CH09_Q007.displayText:
The source explains: Hypoglossal nucleus develops from the basal plate of medulla, and not alar plate.

Option A: Inferior olivary nucleus develops from the alar plate of the medulla.
Option B: Substantia nigra develops from the alar plate of the midbrain.
Option C: Dentate nucleus develops from the alar plate in the cerebellum.

This is the source's classification and the printed key selects the hypoglossal nucleus. Modern developmental accounts describe more complex origins and migrations, particularly for dopaminergic substantia-nigra neurons; the source's broad alar/basal labels should therefore not be treated as universally settled without subject review.

rationales.a: Inferior olivary nucleus is derived from the alar plate of the medulla, so it is not the exception.
rationales.b: Substantia nigra is classified here as an alar-plate derivative of the midbrain.
rationales.c: Dentate nucleus is classified here as an alar-plate derivative associated with cerebellar development.

reconstruction.sourceProblem: The source key selects hypoglossal, but its categorical classification of substantia nigra as an alar-plate derivative is not definitive in current developmental accounts; dopaminergic substantia-nigra neurons are described with complex ventral midbrain origins.
reconstruction.reconstructedContent: Retain the source-keyed answer D and explain the source's classification without presenting it as universally settled; do not silently change the answer key.
evidenceBasis: Immutable Anatomy ED8 source question, options, key and explanation for marrow__ANAT_CH09_Q007 (source PDF question/explanation pages 147 and 155).
Current developmental review describes midbrain dopaminergic neuron development from ventral midbrain progenitor domains; DOI 10.3389/fnana.2020.00032.
Recent peer-reviewed multi-neuromeric fate-mapping work documents substantia nigra/ventral tegmental origins distributed across developmental domains; DOI 10.3389/fnana.2025.1612529.
reconstruction.reviewNote: Answer remains source-keyed for this candidate batch. A medical subject reviewer should decide whether the distractor classification is acceptable for the intended exam level or whether the question needs a visible ambiguity note / answerability gate.

marrow__ANAT_CH09_Q008.takeaway: The anterior commissure is the first cerebral commissure to develop.
marrow__ANAT_CH09_Q008.displayText:
The first commissure to develop is the anterior commissure.

Commissures are fibre bundles that cross the midline and connect the right and left brain hemispheres. Many important fibre bundles cross at lamina terminalis.

Commissures at lamina terminalis:
• Anterior commissure - first commissure to appear. These fibers connect the olfactory bulb and related brain areas to the corresponding structures in the contralateral hemisphere.
• Hippocampal commissure (fornix commissure) - develops second. The fibers emerge from the hippocampus and reach the lamina terminalis. From here, they arch outside the choroid fissure to the mammillary body and the hypothalamus.
• Corpus callosum - appears by the 10th week. It connects the non-olfactory areas of the right and the left cerebral cortices.

Commissures at other areas are:
• Posterior commissure
• Habenular commissure
• Optic chiasma

rationales.a: The hippocampal or fornix commissure develops after the anterior commissure.
rationales.c: The corpus callosum develops later, appearing by approximately the tenth week.
rationales.d: The posterior commissure is a commissural pathway but is not the first commissure to appear.

marrow__ANAT_CH09_Q009.takeaway: The corpus callosum develops through the commissural plate of the lamina terminalis.
marrow__ANAT_CH09_Q009.displayText:
The structure marked as A in the image is the corpus callosum. It develops from the lamina terminalis.

Lamina terminalis is a part of the wall of the neural tube that closes the cranial end of the prosencephalon. The lamina terminalis becomes thickened to form the commissural plate that facilitates the passage of neurons between the two hemispheres.

There are 3 commissures that pass through lamina terminalis:
• Anterior commissure
• Hippocampal commissure
• Corpus callosum

The corpus callosum is the largest of these commissures. Initially, corpus callosum forms a small bundle in the lamina terminalis. Due to the continuous expansion, it extends anteriorly and posteriorly arching over the thin roof of the diencephalon. It connects the non-olfactory areas of the right and the left cerebral cortices.

rationales.a: Basal lamina is not the commissural plate from which the corpus callosum develops.
rationales.b: The alar lamina forms predominantly sensory derivatives of the neural tube and is not the source of the corpus callosum.
rationales.d: The basal plate forms predominantly motor neural-tube derivatives, not the interhemispheric corpus callosum.

marrow__ANAT_CH09_Q010.takeaway: Septum pellucidum is the thin membrane extending between the corpus callosum and fornix.
marrow__ANAT_CH09_Q010.displayText:
Septum pellucidum extends between the corpus callosum and the fornix.

The septum pellucidum is a membrane separating the anterior horns of the left and right lateral ventricles of the brain. It extends from the corpus callosum to the fornix.

It develops from the lamina terminalis. The part of the lamina terminalis that stretches between corpus callosum and fornix persists as septum pellucidum.

rationales.a: The septum pellucidum does not span between anterior and posterior commissures.
rationales.b: The anterior commissure is not the inferior attachment of the septum pellucidum; the fornix is.
rationales.c: Although the fornix is one boundary, the opposite boundary is the corpus callosum rather than the anterior commissure.

marrow__ANAT_CH09_Q011.takeaway: Spina bifida denotes spinal neural-tube defects associated with failure of vertebral arches to fuse.
marrow__ANAT_CH09_Q011.displayText:
Spina bifida is characterized by gaps in the vertebral arches.

Spina bifida is a general term used for neural tube defects affecting the spinal region and associated with splitting of the vertebral arches. It may or may not involve the underlying neural tissue.

There are 3 types of spina bifida, as shown in the source image.

Rachischisis is the most severe type of neural tube defect, where the entire neural tube fails to close. Rachischisis can occur in the spinal cord or brain regions of the neural tube. The exposed neural tissues often become necrotic.

rationales.a: Encephalocele is a cranial defect through which meninges and sometimes brain tissue herniate, not a vertebral-arch gap.
rationales.c: Hydranencephaly involves destructive absence of much of the cerebral hemispheres and is not defined by non-fusion of vertebral arches.
rationales.d: Syringomyelia is a cavitary disorder within the spinal cord and does not describe a gap in the vertebral arches.

marrow__ANAT_CH09_Q012.takeaway: Encephalocele is herniation of meninges with or without neural tissue through a skull defect, most often occipital.
marrow__ANAT_CH09_Q012.displayText:
The image shows a newborn with encephalocele.

Encephaloceles are caused due to defects in the skull through which the meninges and/or neural tissue herniate. The squamous part of the occipital bone is the most frequently affected bone. The bone may be partially or totally lacking.

Based on the degree of defect and tissues herniating, they are classified as follows:
• Meningocele - defect is small and only meninges bulge through it
• Meningoencephalocele - defect is large and a part of brain bulges with the meninges
• Meningohydroencephalocele - defect is large and a part of the brain and ventricle bulge with the meninges

rationales.a: Spina bifida is a spinal vertebral-arch defect rather than a cranial herniation through the skull.
rationales.b: Rachischisis is failure of neural-tube closure with exposed neural tissue, not the localized skull herniation shown.
rationales.d: Myelocele is an open spinal dysraphism involving exposed spinal neural tissue, not a cranial encephalocele.

marrow__ANAT_CH09_Q013.takeaway: Anencephaly follows failed cranial neural-tube closure, exposure and degeneration of the developing brain.
marrow__ANAT_CH09_Q013.displayText:
The image shows the congenital defect of anencephaly.

Failure of the cranial end of the neural tube to close is known as exencephaly. As a result of this, the skull vault does not form. This leaves the malformed brain exposed.

The exposed brain tissue degenerates, leaving a mass of necrotic tissue. This defect with the absence of a major portion of the brain, skull, and scalp is known as anencephaly. The brain stem remains intact.

In some cases, the closure defect of the neural tube extends caudally, and the spinal cord is affected. This condition is known as craniorachischisis, where there is anencephaly plus a large defect involving the spine.

rationales.a: Encephalocele is herniation through a focal skull defect rather than widespread absence of cranial vault and brain tissue.
rationales.b: Spina bifida is a spinal dysraphism characterized by vertebral-arch defects, not the cranial anomaly shown.
rationales.d: Meningoencephalocele contains meninges and brain herniating through a skull defect; it does not represent the extensive destructive cranial defect of anencephaly.

marrow__ANAT_CH09_Q014.takeaway: The stem's fourth-ventricle cystic enlargement and aperture atresia point to the source-keyed diagnosis, Dandy-Walker malformation.
marrow__ANAT_CH09_Q014.displayText:
Blockage of the medial and the lateral apertures of the 4th ventricle is seen in Dandy-Walker syndrome (DWS).

DWS is congenital hydrocephalus associated with atresia of the median aperture (foramen of Magendie) and lateral aperture (foramen of Luschka) of the 4th ventricle. This causes enlargement of the 4th ventricle and hydrocephalus.

The other associated defects seen in DWS include:
• Agenesis of the cerebellar vermis
• Agenesis of the splenium of corpus callosum

The source's aperture-atresia explanation reflects the historical account. Current descriptions emphasize abnormal rhombencephalic-roof development and variable vermian hypoplasia; failed fenestration of the fourth-ventricle outlets remains one possible mechanism rather than a complete, settled explanation. The source-listed splenium agenesis is an associated finding, not required by this stem.
emphasis: This causes enlargement of the 4th ventricle

rationales.a: Syringomyelia is a fluid-filled cavity within the spinal cord and does not cause congenital cystic dilatation of the fourth ventricle from aperture atresia.
rationales.b: Rachischisis is severe failure of neural-tube closure with exposed neural tissue, not obstruction of fourth-ventricle outlets.
rationales.d: Arnold-Chiari malformation involves downward displacement of hindbrain structures through the foramen magnum and is distinct from the fourth-ventricle outlet atresia described here.

reconstruction.sourceProblem: The item states aperture blockage as the cause of Dandy-Walker syndrome, reflecting a historical causal account that current sources describe as incomplete/outdated.
reconstruction.reconstructedContent: Keep the source-keyed diagnosis while distinguishing the source's aperture-atresia description from current accounts centered on rhombencephalic-roof and vermian developmental abnormalities.
